10327-alias-the-lone-wolf:
Louis Joseph Vance published this thriller in 1921, the fourth Lone Wolf story, though each book stands alone. Its hero is Michael Lanyard, a reformed jewel thief known as the Lone Wolf, who now finds trouble even when he seeks quiet. A guest, a charge of guilt, and walking papers open the plot.

Lanyard must clear his name, dodge old foes, and use his skill with locks, disguise, and nerve to stay free. The pace is quick, with chases, traps, and close escapes in the manner of early crime fiction. Readers get a stylish, fast tale of a gentleman thief turned reluctant hero.
11041-the-half-back-a-story-of-school-fo:
Ralph Henry Barbour wrote this school story about Joel, a boy in a straw hat who arrives at Hillton Academy and tries football and golf. Teased at first as a country boy, Joel earns his place through practice, a golf tournament, a broken bell rope, and games against St. Eustace. Later chapters follow him to Harwell, where a varsity place and the great game against Yates await.

Barbour fills the book with practice games, coaches, boat races, and the Goodwin scholarship, all in the spirit of honest, manly sport the dedication praises. Illustrations by B. West Clinedinst picture leaps, drives over Rocky Bunker, and boat crews lifting their shell. The novel remains a classic of American school fiction, warm about teamwork and fair play.
13131-the-were-wolf:
Clemence Housman's 1896 tale, with six plates by Laurence Housman, sets a were-wolf story in a great farm hall in the far north. The hall is ablaze with firelight, noisy with work, and home to little Rol with his puppy and old Trella at her knitting. Into this household comes White Fell, a stranger whose beauty hides a beast.

Christian, one of twin brothers, follows wolf tracks across an ice-bound stream straight to the farm door, where the trail ends in snow. Love, jealousy, and dread then pull the brothers apart, as Sweyn too loves White Fell. Housman's tale is short, stark, and eerie, a folk horror told in plain prose with a cold northern bite.
14445-confidences-talks-with-a-young-gir:
Edith B. Lowry, a Chicago physician, wrote this 1919 book of talks for a young girl about her own body, addressed to a listener called Violet. Lowry dedicated it to the daughters of friends.

Chapters move from flowers and birds to human birth, using nests, ovules, and the womb as gentle analogies for reproduction and growth. Lowry explains monthly changes, rest, sleep, and care of the body in plain, reassuring language. The book reflects early twentieth-century sex education for girls: modest, maternal, and frank by the standards of its day.
18417-the-great-panjandrum-himself:
Randolph Caldecott's picture book tells the nonsense tale of the Great Panjandrum himself, published by Frederick Warne and Company in London. The book is made of pictures with short lines of verse, so the story unfolds as much in image as in word. A woman goes into the garden to cut a cabbage leaf to make an apple pie, and a great she-bear comes down the street and pops its head into the shop.

What, no soap, the tale asks, and the pictures carry the joke forward: a death, an imprudent marriage to the barber, and guests present at the wedding. Children get Caldecott's nonsense at its best: a pie, a bear, a barber, and a wedding, told in pictures that reward looking again. The book belongs with his other picture books, made to be read aloud and laughed over.
21644-every-man-for-himself:
Hopkins Moorhouse opens Every Man for Himself in fog on Front Street, Toronto, in a tale copyrighted in Canada in 1920. A lone policeman writes in his patrol book under an arc light. A young athlete strides out of the gray vapour toward the docks.

Chapters turn on a tan satchel that keeps reappearing at key moments. A listening stenographer, a private car named Obaska, and trouble on the Winnipeg Express drive the plot. Kendrick makes a touchdown, McCorquodale explains, and a race begins. Moorhouse, who wrote Deep Furrows of the prairie west, here spins a brisk tale of money and mystery.
22526-cubs-of-the-wolf:
Cubs of the Wolf is a science fiction story preserved from Project Gutenberg. Its characters argue about ridicule aimed at their own profession. Specialists, one complains, are the butt of enough ridicule already now.

Do something foolish, he warns, and the ridicule follows for life. Knees knock whenever anyone inquires about your specialty afterward. Worse, they threaten to read your thesis aloud in public. That academic dread gives the tale a wry, knowing start. Wolf cubs, by the title, suggest young predators or young trainees. Readers get a period story where status anxiety meets strange science. Its humor comes from experts fearing embarrassment more than danger.
2377-the-son-of-the-wolf:
Jack London's first book, The Son of the Wolf, collects stories of the Yukon gold rush, where men and dogs fight cold, hunger, and each other. The tales include The White Silence and An Odyssey of the North, with London's stark prose already at full power. The north is beautiful, brutal, and indifferent to human plans.

These stories made London's name, drawing on his own Klondike winter. Their themes of endurance and instinct run through all his later work. Readers of adventure fiction will find a powerful debut. London wrote these stories after a winter he spent prospecting in the Klondike.
23988-the-man-who-lost-himself:
H. De Vere Stacpoole, author of The Blue Lagoon and The Gold Trail, published The Man Who Lost Himself in New York in 1918. It opens on the first of June, with Victor Jones of Philadelphia in the Savoy Hotel lounge in London, beaten in his first great battle with life.

Jones is no American in accent: Australian born, he started in a Melbourne bank, went to India for a trading house, and started for himself. Contents run from Jones and the stranger, through Carlton House Terrace and the point of the joke, to the net, the coal mine, and the girl in the Victoria. An attack, a second honeymoon, a mental trap, and a family council lead at last to the chapter He Finds Himself.
24585-the-story-of-cole-younger-by-himse:
Cole Younger wrote his own story, published at Chicago in 1903, as an autobiography of the Missouri guerrilla captain and outlaw. Its subtitle promises his capture and prison life, and the only authentic account of the Northfield raid ever published. Chapters follow his boyhood, the dark and bloody ground of border war, and being driven from home.

Later chapters cover Lone Jack, Quantrell on war, the Palmyra butchery, Lawrence, Belle Starr, and a price on his head. Younger tells his tale in his own voice, defending and explaining a violent life. Readers get a firsthand outlaw memoir, frank, partisan, and unlike any other account of the border wars.
24787-the-south-of-france-east-half:
C. B. Black's guide to the South of France, East Half, covers the Rhone valley, the Riviera coast, and the passes into Italy. Towns from Marseilles to Leghorn appear, with Italian stops at Turin, Florence, Pisa, and Bologna, and maps and plans through the text. A note explains the hotel marks: figures rank houses first or second class, and a star marks the best of its class.

Entries give hard facts for travelers: Toulon's naval arsenal with its ropery and forge fires, its theatres, and its Provencal street life. Black knew the ground himself, and his notes carry the voice of a man who walked the towns. The guide still works as a portrait of the Riviera and Provence in the age of rail travel.
26003-jesus-himself:
Rev. Andrew Murray offers brief messages on knowing Jesus himself, revised from two addresses first printed in the South African Pioneer, organ of the Cape General Mission. Printed by Revell in 1893, the book takes for its text Luke's words that their eyes were opened and they knew him. Murray says it is possible to have Jesus with us and never know it, and to preach and hear all truth about him yet miss him.

Later messages press the same point for strugglers who fear fresh failure in a holy life, amid difficulties, temptations, and weak character. Murray longs to tell them of a presence that abides every moment, Jesus himself as portion forever. The book is short, devout, and plain, meant for readers who seek a closer walk.
26741-i-m-a-stranger-here-myself:
Mack Reynolds wrote this short story of Tangier. Its tagline warns that one cannot be too careful about the people one meets there, since they are all weirdies of one kind or another. Its narrator, Rupert, sits at the Cafe de Paris on the Place de France. The square marks the end of Boulevard Pasteur and the start of Rue de la Liberté toward the Grand Socco and the medina.

A three-minute walk carries Tangier from a modern, California-like resort to Harun al-Rashid's Baghdad. King-size sidewalk cafes serve draft beer and shoeshines for thirty Moroccan francs. Berber, Rif, Arab, Senegalese, Chinese, Hindu, Turk, Levantine, Filipino, and European pass in native costume and European dress. Smugglers, fugitives, con men, spies, ex-royalty, and subversives crowd the cafes, where Rupert and Paul talk satellites, flying saucers, and the Paris Herald Tribune.
27202-wagner-the-wehr-wolf:
George W. M. Reynolds's Wagner, the Wehr-Wolf opens in January 1516, on a dark and tempestuous night in the great Black Forest of Germany. Thunder growls, lightning flashes, and streams rush with deafening din among huge oaks, firs, and howling wolves.

An old man of ninety sits in his cottage on the forest's verge, bald, toothless, and white-bearded, alone in the world. Wife, children, grandchildren, and all relations save one have preceded him on the long last voyage, and that one will draw him into the tale of the wehr-wolf.
31930-the-song-of-the-wolf:
Frank Mayer's 1910 novel The Song of the Wolf, published in New York by Moffat, Yard and Company, opens with a landscape in perfect harmony. A turquoise sky blends with sprouting grass and budding sagebrush, aspens lie silver-gray against a tawny mountain, and a coyote slinks among deserted prairie-dog mounds.

Its twelve chapters run from a rift in the lute and the mark of the beast through alarms, Belshazzar, a passing cloud, and frenzied finance. Readers get a western novel of the open range, told in richly colored prose, where nature's harmony is broken by human greed and passion.
32465-the-whelps-of-the-wolf:
George Marsh's northern novel, copyrighted in 1922, opens in the land of the Windigo and follows a trail that ends, then begins again, through home, love, and danger. Early chapters introduce Julie Breton, the moon of flowers, a friend of demons, and a long trail to the south coast. A meeting in the marshes, a camp on the Ghost, and warnings in the wind build toward the work of white wolves and the mark of the breed.

Later chapters bring starving moons, spring and Fleur, ice going soft, a dead man's tale, and Inspector Wallace taking charge. Cree justice, the fangs of half-breeds, and the voice of the Windigo close a story of dogs, men, and the far frontiers. Marsh writes vividly about the Canadian north, where loyalty to a dog can test loyalty to a person.
32499-to-a-skull-on-my-bookshelf:
Elizabeth Virginia Raplee's poem, printed in Weird Tales in October 1937, addresses a skull kept on the speaker's bookshelf. The bony relic of forgotten days dominates the room, its empty sockets following the speaker with a sardonic gaze in deepening gloom. The speaker wonders what secret, grisly jest the skull grins at, and what it has learned of the dark realm to which all people are addressed.

Raplee then asks by what rude hands the skull was exhumed and wrenched from its body in its earthy bed. The speaker fears the same indignity after death: strangely resurrected, the speaker too may adorn the wall or desk of someone yet unborn. In short compass, the poem turns a household curiosity into a meditation on death, dignity, and the future.
32502-what-happened-to-inger-johanne-as-:
Dikken Zwilgmeyer's What Happened to Inger Johanne, translated from Norwegian by Emilie Poulsson and published in Boston in October 1919, tells a Norwegian girl's life in her own voice. A frontispiece shows Mina and Inger Johanne hauling a girl up by the arms into a boat. Chapters introduce ourselves, our town, and other things, an interrupted celebration, a first journey alone, and what happened one St. John's Day.

Later chapters cover being left behind, hiding in a meal chest, pets and especially Carola-Carolus, Christmas mumming, Mother Brita's grandchild, and the mason's little pigs. Locked in, a trip to Goodfields saeter, lost in the forest, travelling with a billy-goat, school, a circus, and moving follow. Florence Liley Young illustrated a warm, lively girls' book of Norwegian country life.
32534-neighbors-life-stories-of-the-othe:
Jacob A. Riis's Neighbors, published in New York in 1914, gathers life stories from the tenements he called the other half. A landlord's demand opens the first tale, where Judah Kapelowitz and his wife face eviction two months behind on rent after six years of struggle in the Promised Land.

Later stories follow families, widows, children, and neighbors through rent, work, sickness, and Christmas kindness. Riis writes with close attention to speech, rooms, and small acts of help, showing how people in crowded streets find dignity, quarrel, forgive, and carry one another through hard seasons.
350-fanny-herself:
Edna Ferber follows Fanny Brandeis, a bright Jewish girl in a small Wisconsin town, in this novel. Fanny grows up above her mother's store, helps at home, and dreams of a wider life. When loss and need press her, she must choose between duty to kin and her own urge to work and write.

Ferber, in a teasing preface, mocks novels that drag a heroine from cradle to altar in full detail. Her own tale moves briskly through school, shop, and city newsrooms. The book charms as a portrait of a plucky young woman finding her place, with humor, grit, and a keen eye for town life.
35006-an-experimental-translocation-of-t:
Four wildlife men wrote this report on moving eastern timber wolves to a new home ground. Thomas Weise, William Robinson, and Richard Hook taught at Northern Michigan University. David Mech served the Fish and Wildlife Service in its rare wildlife work.

The Fish and Wildlife Service's Region 3 office at Fort Snelling sent out the report. Its parts run in order: the study ground, the methods, and the results. Social structure of the wolves gets its own head in the results. Such trials test if a rare beast can be set down where it once lived and left to breed. Park and forest men use reports like this to plan their own moves.
36998-every-man-for-himself:
Norman Duncan, who wrote Doctor Luke of the Labrador, set these tales on that same hard coast. Harper printed Every Man for Himself in September 1908. The pieces had run in Harper's, Outlook, and Century in the years just before.

The Wayfarer leads the set, then A Matter of Expediency. The Minstrel, the Squall, and the Fool of Skeleton Tickle fill the middle. A Comedy of Candlestick Cove and By-an'-by Brown of Blunder Cove keep the local colour. They Who Lose at Love and the Revolution at Satan's Trap close the list. A front plate shows a girl promised to Slow Jim Tool, in the plain speech of the coast Duncan loved.
37323-poems-on-golf:
Poems on Golf was printed at Edinburgh for private circulation in 1867. Some members of the Edinburgh Burgess Golfing Society resolved to gather and print a few fugitive pieces in verse on the game. The poems and songs were procured after some labour.

The contents open with The Goff, an heroi comical poem. Golfiana holds an address to St Andrews, The Golfiad, and the first hole at St Andrews on a crowded day. Another peep at the links and the nine holes of St Andrews Links follow. Songs hold The Golfers Garland, The Links of Innerleven, and In Praise of Gutta Percha. Far and Sure, Gae Bring My Guid Auld Clubs, and When Tom and Me Were Laddies close the set. A list of subscribers names the members. Golf fans get the game young songbook.
37394-fifty-years-of-golf:
Horace G Hutchinson looked back on half a century of golf in Fifty Years of Golf, first published in nineteen nineteen. Hutchinson was the first English captain of the Royal and Ancient club. A note added in nineteen nineteen says the war delayed the book but changed little in it.

Early chapters tell how golf grew in England and recall Young Tommy Morris and other great players. Hutchinson writes from his own life in the game, and he owns that such a book must use the word I a great deal. Course tales, matches, and the men who shaped the sport fill the rest.
41149-the-soul-of-golf:
The Soul of Golf is a book on the game by Vaile, printed by Macmillan in London in 1912. Vaile had already written Modern Golf and Modern Lawn Tennis. A front plate shows George Duncan, the young Hanger Hill professional, praised as one of the finest golfers alive.

Vaile begins with the soul and the mystery of golf, then turns to craft. Putting takes a long chapter, and fallacies of golf another. He weighs the placing of weight, the power of the left side, and the work of the eyes. The master stroke and the action of the wrists get chapters of their own. He closes with the flight of the ball, the ball itself, the making of clubs, and the literature of golf. It is a thinker's manual from the game's great age of theory.
46460-gunboat-and-gun-runner-a-tale-of-t:
Gunboat and Gun Runner, a tale of the Persian Gulf by Surgeon Rear Admiral Jeans, was issued by Blackie in 1914. Pictures by Padday illustrate the boys’ adventure. A plate shows the Bunder Abbas coming upon an Arab dhow in the act. The dhow is landing guns on that page of the tale.

Jeans had written John Graham, Sub Lieutenant, and Ford of the Vigilant before it. His preface opens on the fierce, unruly tribes beyond the shore. British gunboats patrolled the Gulf to choke the arms traffic of those years. Rifles ran by dhow to tribes and rebels across that sea. Jeans knew the patrol from service, and writes it for boys. Chase, boarding, and desert ports fill his yarn.
46893-how-paris-amuses-itself:
How Paris Amuses Itself, by Berkeley Smith, is a light survey of the pleasures of Paris, copyrighted in 1903. Smith had written The Real Latin Quarter before this book. A drawing of a cheap cafe concert in Montmartre fronts the volume. That scene sets the tone of the whole tour.

Smith takes the reader through the playhouses, cafes, and dance halls of Paris. He writes as an American who knows the city by night and day. Cheap shows and grand ones get their turn in his pages. The Latin Quarter, the boulevards, and the hill of Montmartre supply his ground. Such books sold Paris to tourists as a city of fun. Smith keeps the tone bright, with an eye for the cheap seats as well as the boxes.
5078-when-a-man-comes-to-himself:
Woodrow Wilson's When a Man Comes to Himself describes the moment a person stops living wholly preoccupied with his own powers, interests, and petty plans centered on himself. He clears his eyes to see the world as it is, and his own true place and function in it, in a process Wilson calls disillusionment.

The scales fall away, and the man sees himself soberly, learning under what conditions his powers must act and what his powers actually are. He sheds earlier prepossessions, both too favorable and too unfavorable, from nursery and from youthful reading. Readers get a short essay on maturity, written by a future president about the education of character.
5114-ardath-the-story-of-a-dead-self:
Marie Corelli's Ardath follows a sceptical poet whose life is overturned by a vision of a lost world. The first part, Saint and Sceptic, sets his doubt against faith. The second, In Al-Kyris, carries him into an ancient city where a former self and an old love return to confront him with the life he has wasted.

Corelli mixes romance, mysticism, and moral warning, asking whether a soul can be reborn from its own dead self. The novel's lush, earnest style made it a bestseller of its day. It still reads as a striking example of Victorian spiritual romance, half ghost story and half sermon on redemption.
54741-a-sailor-in-spite-of-himself:
Harry Castlemon wrote A Sailor in Spite of Himself, published by Henry Coates and Company in Philadelphia in 1898. Castlemon wrote many boys' series, including the Gunboat, Rod and Gun, and Rocky Mountain books. A frontispiece captioned Shanghaied states the plot at a glance: a boy carried off to sea against his will.

The opening chapter stages a sailboat race between the Blues and the Whites, in the Sunbeam and the Firefly. Chapters follow Bob, Gus, and Ben through a lawyer's office, a two-hundred-dollar pearl, and a question over who wrote a codicil. Deserters, a mutiny, and a telegram carry the adventure to its close. Castlemon wrote fast, clean tales of pluck for the boys of his generation.
60075-a-memoir-of-thomas-bewick-written-:
Thomas Bewick wrote this tale of his own life, printed at Newcastle in 1862. It came out for Jane Bewick of Gateshead. The book is dressed with cuts on wood, drawn and cut by the author in his own hand. Those cuts were made for a work on the fish of Britain, and had not been put in print in front of this book. A cut by John Bewick of 1781 shows Cherryburn, the home of the clan.

A word of praise from a man of art stands at the front of the book. Thomas Bewick, it says, was a true first mind: not a man of paint, but an artist of the top rank in his way. His works are of the least size that can be, yet so much of pull is packed in such small space.
60749-a-thousand-mile-walk-to-the-gulf:
Thousand Mile Walk to the Gulf is a nature journal by John Muir, from his 1867 walk. Contents run through Kentucky forests and caves, then across the Cumberland mountains. The river country of Georgia and camping among the tombs fill the middle chapters. Florida swamps and forests lead to Cedar Keys and a sojourn in Cuba.

A portrait of Muir about 1870 and a route map illustrate the posthumous book. He set out on the first of September 1867, parting from home for long, he believed. The young botanist walked to the Gulf studying plants and his own soul. Nature writing holds the journal as the seed of Muir later greatness.
61329-timber-wolf:
Timber Wolf is a western novel by Jackson Gregory of California. Scribner published it in New York in August of the year 1923. Gregory also wrote The Everlasting Whisper and Desert Valley before it. He dedicates the tale to Sue with a line from Julianito. Chapter one opens at Big Pine, a tiny outpost in the wilderness.

Big Pine sits well within the rim of great southwestern wild country. Like other aloof mountain settlements, it knows monotonous quiet most days. Infrequently, for one reason or another, come days of excitement there. At times those days seem to come for no reason whatever. Gregory's tale of the high timber country breaks that quiet soon.
61895-space-wolf:
Space Wolf is a science fiction story by Ray Cummings, first published in Planet Stories in the summer of 1941. Its hero is Solo Morgan, a lone prospector of space. The lure of precious zolonite has drawn him to Titan, Saturn's barren moon.

Morgan works alone by motto and by habit. At twenty-eight he counts himself a failure, for the one big strike he always meant to make has never come. Now his spectroscope and radiometer readings point to a zolonite lode in the heights above his one-man ship. As he climbs toward a plateau of blue-grey vegetation, a shot cracks out and a lead bullet flattens on the rock beside him. Titan was supposed to be uninhabited, and an old-fashioned bullet makes the mystery sharper.
6365-richard-dare-s-venture-or-striking-:
Edward Stratemeyer, author of Oliver Bright's Search and To Alaska for Gold, opens his Bound to Succeed series with Richard Dare's venture. A serious accident frames the start. Richard tells his mother at breakfast that it is high time he found work, for his father grows worse and may soon be unable to work each day. Since finishing school he has felt like a fish out of water, though his mother praises his garden and his neat front fence.

Richard wants regular work and weekly wages, a big help to a household that costs a heap of money to run. The preface notes that boys' books here have found girls and grown readers too. Stratemeyer writes a plain, encouraging tale of a boy striking out for himself, from home chores to city streets, Liberty to Greenwich to Fulton, and the elevated road above them.
67810-friends-on-the-shelf:
Friends on the Shelf, by Bradford Torrey, is a book of essays on beloved authors. Houghton, Mifflin issued it in Boston and New York in 1906. A line from Edward FitzGerald gives the title: I must get back to my friends on the shelf.

The contents name the friends in order: Hazlitt first, then FitzGerald himself, then Thoreau. A second essay weighs Thoreau's demand upon nature. Stevenson and Keats follow, with Anatole France near the end. Shorter pieces treat verbal magic, quotability, and the grace of obscurity. One defends the traveler's notebook, and one laments the lack of an American literature. The Hazlitt essay opens on happiness: the man who enjoys himself holds the true riches. Poverty may share his table, Torrey says, yet his good things are within.
69200-little-jack-rabbit-and-mr-wicked-w:
David Cory wrote Little Jack Rabbit and Mr. Wicked Wolf, in 1923. Grosset and Dunlap at New York put out the bunny book. Barbour illustrated this volume of the trademarked series. The Little Fir Tree opens the contents of the tales. Christmas Eve and Christmas Day follow in the chapter list.

The wicked wolf himself takes the fourth chapter of the contents. The Thinking Cap follows in the list. Santa's Reindeer and Photographer Crane stand in the middle list. The Milky Way, Home Again, and Resolutions follow in order. Here are some Christmas presents, said the little bunny in front. The little fir tree in the wood has been good all year. Winter time is here and Christmas day is very near now. The birds speak of that fir in the verse chapter. Cory gives small children a rabbit's Christmas round.
6925-the-history-of-thomas-ellwood-writt:
Thomas Ellwood, a simple Quaker, tells his own life in this history, introduced by Henry Morley. Morley sets Ellwood beside George Cavendish's Life of Wolsey, since one man loved pomp from within a great household while Ellwood found earth's pomps vain beside the spiritual life. The book charms, Morley says, by the frankness with which Ellwood makes himself known.

That same plain simplicity brings readers nearer than most books bring them to a seventeenth century Friend. Ellwood's tale covers faith, suffering, and daily conduct among Quakers in hard times. It reads as a companion life of quiet conscience, written without flourish and full of direct self knowledge.
69255-of-one-blood-or-the-hidden-self:
Pauline E Hopkins wrote Of One Blood, or The Hidden Self, a novel issued in nineteen hundred and two. The hero, Reuel Briggs, is a young medical student in Boston. The tale opens in the first week of November, in sleet and cold.

Briggs sits alone among his books and tools, in a bare room that serves for living and sleep. He has not eaten or left the room since coming from the hospital. Dark thoughts press on him, and he asks what his hard work is for. The east wind drives sleet at the panes. Loneliness and hidden ties shape the story ahead.
71786-catherine-herself:
Catherine Herself is a novel by James Hilton, first published in London by Fisher Unwin in 1920. Its chapter titles borrow the language of music: prelude, nocturne, crescendo, accelerando, and allegro con fuoco stand among them. Two episodes of a man named Trant frame Catherine's story.

The first chapter opens inside a child's mind. Catherine thinks: day is white, night is black, but sometimes it is half white and half black. There were five knobs on the brass rail of the bed, and one of them would come off. The baker came every night and asked how Cathie was. Blue flames flickered on the coals and seemed to speak. Hilton renders childhood as a stream of small certainties and sounds. The contents then trace her growth through disillusion, tragedy, and loneliness, to success, crisis, and the last phase. It is an early novel by the future author of Lost Horizon.
72042-the-corning-egg-farm-book-by-corni:
The Corning Egg Farm Book, by Corning himself, tells the complete story of the Corning Egg Farm at Bound Brook, New Jersey, from its start to 1912. Gardner Corning published it at the farm in that year. The title promises a full description of the method and system that made this the most famous poultry farm in the world.

The contents trace the farm's building: it started with sixty Buff Rock eggs, then adopted White Leghorns. Chapters cover the first roosting closets, the counting of only livable chicks, and the success of the great flock system. Foreign visitors came, and Germany investigated the farm. Later chapters argue that egg farming is the most profitable branch of poultry keeping. They treat the great layer, eggs for market, and the choice of breed.
73187-memoirs-of-james-hardy-vaux-writte:
Memoirs of James Hardy Vaux is the life of a convict, written by himself and published in London in 1819 in two volumes. The chapter heads map a fall. Vaux tells of his birth and his boyhood to the age of nine. School, grandparents, and shifts of home follow. Friends found him a place at Liverpool on trial. Work at the law in London came next, with lodgings bilked and bills unpaid. Soon he lived by his wits, and served as a hackney waiter.

A trip to Portsmouth turned his course. Talk with a frigate's surgeon led to a post as midshipman. Friends fitted him out with a kind hand, and he joined his ship in delight. He made fast progress in his new craft. Then the hard winter, the harsh duty, and his own bent bent him back.
73960-the-man-who-hated-himself:
The Man Who Hated Himself is a western story by Walt Coburn of Montana. Coburn calls it a powerful story of the Montana cattle trails. The great blizzard of 1886 stands at the heart of the tale. Every stockman in the northwest recalls that hard winter, he opens. It broke most of them, that winter of 1886 to 1887.

One cattleman wintering in the South wrote home about his stock. His line rider drew a starving cow hung up in the drifts. Waiting for a chinook, the last of five thousand, he wrote below. Charlie Russell drew that picture, then a plain cowpuncher himself. The Circle C outfit shipped its last steers about November first. Snow was spitting as they finished loading the cattle train for Chicago. Buck Bell rode up to the wagon boss in the raw wind.
75244-the-shadow-of-the-wolf:
The Shadow of the Wolf, a detective novel by R. Austin Freeman, was copyrighted in 1925 and issued at New York. Its chapters follow Doctor Thorndyke, the famed medical jurist of Freeman’s tales. A woman named Margaret Purcell receives a letter early in the book. She consults a man named Penfield, then confers with Thorndyke himself.

Thorndyke makes a few inquiries, and tries over the moves of the case. A flash note factory enters the plot as a queer trade. A man named Varney prepares a deception and pulls the strings more than once. Penfield receives a shock as the net draws in. Chapter heads promise a medico legal turn near the end. The tale is built on proof, patience, and the slow exposure of a clever fraud.
75756-steppenwolf:
Steppenwolf is a novel by Hermann Hesse, translated from the German by Basil Creighton and published by Henry Holt in New York in 1929. Its main text is called Harry Haller's Records, and it is marked: for madmen only. Haller is a discontented middle-aged man who lives a primitive and retiring life. His account opens with a single ordinary day, recorded hour by hour.

He worked a little, read old books, and had pains for two hours, as elderly people do. A powder relieved them, and a hot bath gave kindly warmth. The post brought undesired letters and circulars three times. He walked for an hour under feathery cloud patterns. Yet the day, he concludes, was not one of rapture or even of happiness. It was one of the lukewarm, bearable days that now make up his life.
76981-saved-from-herself:
Saved from Herself is a story-paper novel by Adelaide Stirling, issued as number 550 of Street and Smith's Eagle Series in New York. Thirty-one chapters carry the tale, from the theatre to the lion's mouth and back. The chapter titles alone sketch a melodrama of the classic kind.

A penniless adventuress and a rose-coloured room open the plot. The mystery, a lucky cast, and a dream of safety follow. Threefold danger, the luck of Marcus Wray, and a vow to possess him or die raise the stakes. A net for her feet, her hour of triumph, and more treachery fill the middle. Circe's eyes, a spinet, and a midnight scene come before the edge of doom. A ghostly eavesdropper, a mother's child, and truth that lied lead to the cry of the title: save me from myself. Stirling's novel is the Eagle Series in full cry.
77510-the-assistant-self:
The Assistant Self, a science fiction story by F L Wallace, turns on a virtue carried too far. Hal Talbot suffers from a crippling weight of empathy. He always sees the other person's side, and so he fumbles every duty and cannot hold any job for long. His girl Laura walks out on him over a missed meeting, and he sits down in a bar to drink.

A well dressed stranger takes the other half of Talbot's booth and begins to talk. The head note states the theme in plain words: a superabundance of a virtue can lead to tragedy. Wallace builds the tale from that seed, asking what a man is to do when his own self will not let him stand his ground. The stranger's counsel promises a way out, at a price the story will name.
78217-the-fate-of-the-wolf:
W C Tuttle wrote this western tale of the Mexican borderland. The Wolf, El Lobo, struck fear into men's hearts there. Once he robbed only the rich to give to the poor; then he turned killer and spoiler of all. Only Destino knew why. The tale opens in Felipe's cantina in the Santa Clemente country.

A tall stranger with red-tinged hair and devil-may-care blue eyes laughs at the crew for jumping at a name. He slaps his broad chaps, calls for beer all round, and wishes aloud for something that could make him shiver. Emilio of the Rancho Sereno starts to name El Lobo, and the stranger laughs till the cobwebs dance. Don Roberto Aliso's rich ranch offers the Wolf his likeliest prize.
7845-toward-the-gulf:
Edgar Lee Masters's Toward the Gulf gathers poems from lake boats and cities of the plain through Johnny Appleseed, the loom, Sir Galahad, and a dialogue at Perko's. Later pieces visit St. Deseret, heaven as an hour, Victor Rafolski on art, and the landscape of tomorrow.

The book also holds a canticle of the race, Black Eagle's return, a room of mirrors, a letter, and a debt paid for Lafayette and Rochambeau. Dedicated in spirit to William Marion Reedy, though Spoon River took the formal dedication, it shows Masters beyond Spoon River, in lyric, satire, and elegy.
7942-little-eyolf:
Henrik Ibsen wrote this three-act play in Christiania during 1894, and it was published in Copenhagen that December. William Archer's English version, printed here, adds an introduction tracing the play's sources, including the rat-wife figure Ibsen remembered from his schooldays in Skien. The household at the centre is Alfred Allmers, his wife Rita, and their young son Eyolf.

Eyolf, already lame from a fall, drowns while his parents are absorbed in each other, and the rest of the play is their reckoning with guilt. Allmers turns toward duty and teaching poor children, while Rita faces her own jealousy and grief. The play is short and stark, and it remains one of Ibsen's most unsettling studies of how a marriage survives, or fails to survive, a child's death.
8187-the-complete-poems-of-sir-thomas-mo:
Sir Thomas Moore collected his complete poems himself, with explanatory notes and a biographical sketch by William M. Rossetti. Moore was born in Dublin on May 28, 1780, to Roman Catholic parents; his father was a grocer and spirit-retailer. And his schooling came from Samuel Whyte, Sheridan's first preceptor, a man of more than average literary culture who encouraged the boy's taste. The poems that follow made Moore the most popular lyricist of his age.

The collection ranges from Irish Melodies, which gave Ireland songs still sung today, to satires, odes, and Eastern romances. Moore's music and wit made him Byron's friend and Ireland's national bard. For poetry readers, this self-collected edition is the authoritative Moore, and a treasury of early nineteenth-century song.
9052-the-golden-calf:
Mary Elizabeth Braddon wrote this novel of money, marriage, and social climbing in Victorian England. Its heroine, Ida, prays with clasped hands in the frontispiece scene, caught between love and the lure of wealth. Chapters follow an articled pupil, a vow to marry for money, and life at Wendover Abbey.

Braddon, famed for Lady Audley's Secret, spins a tale of ambition and its costs. Lady Palliser studies the upper ten. Fruits fail, love dies, and time ranges on. The novel still pleases as a brisk sensation tale with a sharp eye for class.
981-beowulf:
An anonymous Anglo-Saxon poet sang Beowulf, here translated by Francis Gummere. The poem opens with praise of the prowess of people-kings of spear-armed Danes. It praises Scyld the Scefing, who tore the mead-bench from foes and awed the earls, though he lay friendless as a foundling at first.

Beowulf, a Geat hero, sails to Denmark to slay Grendel, the monster who haunts Heorot hall, then faces Grendel's mother and, in old age, a dragon. Gummere's verse keeps the old alliterative music. The poem stands as the greatest work of Old English literature, and a founding tale of heroism in the West.
alias-the-lone-wolf: Louis Joseph Vance revives his gentleman thief in Alias the Lone Wolf, a yarn of daring, disguise, and romance. The Lone Wolf moves through a world of jewel theft, pursuit, and clever escapes, with Vance's smooth, cinematic pace. The novel belongs to the popular crime-romance of its era, where a charming rogue outwits both police and rivals.
ardath-the-story-of-a-dead-self:
Marie Corelli's Ardath: The Story of a Dead Self opens in a monastery deep in the Caucasus. A storm gathers over the Pass of Dariel as night approaches, and Mount Kazbek rises coldly white. Part one bears the title Saint and Sceptic. The sceptic is Theos Alwyn, a young poet whose fame has not saved his faith.

Alwyn seeks the monk Heliobas, whose learning joins holiness to strange science. Under his guidance the poet's spirit travels to Al-Kyris, a lost city of the ancient world. There he meets the self he was in a former life, and the woman he loved and wronged. Corelli builds her romance on reincarnation and the soul's long education. Ardath was her most ambitious occult novel, preached with a prophet's certainty. Its Caucasus storm and phantom city frame a gospel of spiritual evolution.
beowulf:
Francis Barton Gummere translated Beowulf, the Old English epic of the Geatish hero, into alliterative English verse that keeps the original's hammering rhythm. The prelude praises Scyld Scefing, founder of the Danish house, who waxed under heaven until far peoples gave him gifts. His descendant Hrothgar builds Heorot, the great hall Grendel attacks.

Beowulf crosses the whale-path to Denmark, wrestles Grendel in the gabled hall, dives to fight Grendel's mother, and in old age faces a dragon at home. Gummere's diction, athelings, mead-benches, and hall-thanes, gives modern readers the poem's strangeness without a crib. His version served generations of students as the standard verse translation of England's oldest epic.
britannica-1911-aard-wolf: Aard-wolf, or earth-wolf, is the subject of a short entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The entry names a South and East African mammal, Proteles cristatus, in the flesh-eating order. In looks it recalls a small striped hyena, but with a sharper muzzle and keener ears. A long mane that can stand on end runs down the neck and back. The beast works by night and burrows by day. Its food is spoiled flesh, grubs, and termites.
britannica-1911-arculf:
Arculf was a Gallic bishop and pilgrim who travelled to the Levant about six eighty, says a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry. He was the first Christian traveller of note in the Near East after the rise of Islam. On his way home, contrary winds drove him to Britain.

He came to Iona, where he told his tale to the abbot Adamnan. Adamnan wrote the account out and gave it to a Northumbrian king at York. Bede later made a short form of it, and a longer digest as well. That digest became a famed guide to the Holy Places for the middle ages. Arculf first noted a column at Jerusalem said to mark the centre of the world. He also described holy sites, Alexandria, and Constantinople.
britannica-1911-arnulf:
Arnulf, a Roman emperor who lived from about 850 to 899, is profiled in a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. He was the unlawful son of Carloman, king of Bavaria and Italy. About 876 he was made margrave of Carinthia, and his rank and lands were confirmed in 880. The lack of lawful male heirs among the later Carolingians raised his standing.

He did homage to the emperor Charles the Fat in 882, the entry says. The next years he spent in constant war with the Slavs and the Northmen. In 887 he joined the disgust felt at Charles's lack of capacity. He marched with a large army, Charles gave up the throne, and the Germans recognised Arnulf as king. A famed historian called that the first free act of the German secular world.
britannica-1911-backhuysen-ludolf:
Backhuysen, Ludolf (1631-1708), was a Dutch painter born at Emden in Hanover and raised for a merchant's life at Amsterdam. A strong gift for painting turned him from business to art, studying first under Allart van Everdingen and then under Hendrik Dubbels, two leading masters of the day.

Sea-pieces made his name. An eager student of nature, Backhuysen often went out in an open boat in rough weather to watch the effects of tempests at first hand. His many compositions are nearly all variations on that one subject, in a style of intense realism, faithful copying of nature. In later years he turned to etching and calligraphy. He died at Amsterdam in November 1708.
britannica-1911-bastian-adolf:
Adolf Bastian (1826– ), a German ethnologist born at Bremen, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Educated as a physician, he gave his early years to travel. He sailed to Australia as a ship's surgeon in 1851 and visited almost every part of the world before returning in 1859. A five-year expedition to the Far East followed in 1861. Back in Berlin he became professor of ethnology at the university and keeper of its ethnological museum.

Publishing made Bastian a founder of his science. His Peoples of Eastern Asia filled six volumes as an immense storehouse of facts. Der Mensch in der Geschichte had come earlier, in 1860. He succeeded Virchow as president of the Berlin Anthropological Society and helped form the German Africa Society in 1878. He edited the Zeitschrift für Ethnologie from 1869, and kept travelling in Africa, South America, and India. Works on Buddhism, America, and Indonesia fill the closing list.
britannica-1911-baumbach-rudolf:
Rudolf Baumbach (1840–1905), a German poet born at Kranichfeld in Thuringia, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was the son of a country doctor and was schooled at the gymnasium of Meiningen. After science studies he worked as a private tutor in Austrian towns: Graz, Brünn, Görz, and Triest. In Triest an Alpine legend, Zlatorog, in 1877, caught the taste of the public. His Songs of a Journeyman followed in 1878, and both fixed his choice of a life in letters.

Song and tale were his twin gifts. In 1885 he went home to Meiningen as ducal librarian. He was a poet of the breezy, wandering school, and wrote fine drinking songs after Scheffel's manner. His Die Lindenwirtin won him a lasting place with German students. His real strength lay in verse tales, above all of his native Thuringia. Frau Holde and the Thüringer Lieder are named among them.
britannica-1911-calf:
Calf is an English word with two main senses. This short 1911 Britannica entry explains both of them. The first sense is the young of certain animals. It means the young of the cattle family above all. It also covers the young of the elephant. Whales and seals have calves too, in common speech. The word appears in German as Kalb and in Dutch as kalf.

The same word names a small island by a larger one. The Calf of Man is the stock example. It also names a mass of ice broken from an iceberg. The second sense is part of the human leg. It is the fleshy back of the leg, between knee and ankle. Its origin is unknown, the entry says. A Celtic word for a leg may lie behind it. The whole notice is brief, and it rests on word history alone.
britannica-1911-cnwulf:
Cœnwulf, king of Mercia who died in 821, is given a short reign entry in the 1911 Britannica. He took the throne in 796 on the death of Ecgfrith, son of Offa. His rise stood out, since his line had not held the throne for six rounds of kin. In 798 he marched into Kent, deposed and jailed Eadberht Praen, and set his own brother Cuthred on that throne.

Cuthred ruled Kent till 807, then Cœnwulf held it himself. In his reign the archbishopric of Lichfield was done away with. His long quarrel with Wulfred of Canterbury outlasted him and was settled only in 825. He died in 821 and was followed by his brother Ceolwulf the First.
britannica-1911-continental-shelf:
Continental Shelf is a geography article from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The term names the sunken platform on which a continent or island stands. The entry explains the idea with a simple picture. A coin sunk partway in water shows the shape well.

The raised image on the coin stands for the dry continent and its islands. The flat sunken rim around it plays the part of the shelf. The coin's edge marks where the deep begins, the continental slope. The article then divides the earth's surface into three zones. Continent heights and ocean depths are the first two. Between them lies a border zone, cut nearly in half by the coast line. Half of that zone lies under less than a hundred fathoms of water. The rest runs deeper, and the entry gives its measure too.
britannica-1911-dahlgren-john-adolf:
John Adolf Dahlgren is the subject of a life entry in the 1911 Britannica. He was an admiral in the navy of the United States. He lived from 1809 to 1870 and was born in Philadelphia. His father was the Swedish consul in that city. He joined the navy in the year 1826. He saw service in the Civil War at sea.

He was most famed as a scholar of guns and fire power. Skill in numbers put him on coast survey work in 1834. Weak eyes forced him to rest for some years. In 1847 he moved to the ordnance branch of the navy. There he worked to make the guns of the fleet better. A smooth bore gun of his design bore his name. Its round shape won it a soda bottle nickname.
britannica-1911-elf: Elf is a small spirit being in old Teutonic tales. A short entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica sets it apart from fairies. Elves were held sly and harmful more often than kind. They were blamed for sickness and bad dreams at night. Tales said they stole children and left changelings in their place. Flint arrowheads found in fields were called elf bolts or elf arrows. People thought elves shot cattle with those stone points. A tangle in hair was called an elf lock for the same reason.
britannica-1911-flambard-ranulf:
Ranulf Flambard, who died in 1128, was bishop of Durham and chief minister of William Rufus. He was son of a Norman parish priest of the diocese of Bayeux. He came young to England and entered the chancery of William I. The barons disliked him and nicknamed him Flambard, the torch-bearer, for his skill as a mischief-maker. He won fame as a sharp financier. He also seems to have played a large part in compiling the Domesday survey.

Early in Rufus's reign Flambard returned to royal service as the king's chaplain. He headed the chancery and kept the great seal, though in effect he was a treasurer. Chroniclers tie his name to the clever methods of extortion used between 1087 and 1100. He farmed vacant church posts for the king and took the see of Durham in 1099. Under Henry I his fortune broke, and he was imprisoned.
britannica-1911-glassbrenner-adolf:
Adolf Glassbrenner, a German humorist and satirist who lived from 1810 to 1876, is profiled in this 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. Born in Berlin in March 1810, he worked briefly in a merchant's office before turning to journalism. In 1831 he edited a paper called Don Quixote. It was shut down in 1833 for its radical bent.

Writing as Adolf Brennglas, Glassbrenner published a long series of sketches of Berlin life. Those sketches made him the founder of a popular satirical writing tied to modern Berlin. In 1848 he entered politics and led the democrats in Mecklenburg-Strelitz. Driven out in 1850, he lived in Hamburg and later edited a Berlin paper. The article also lists his comic verse, poems, and comic epics, and notes his death in Berlin in 1876.
britannica-1911-glauber-johann-rudolf:
Johann Rudolf Glauber (1604-1668) was a German chemist, and this 1911 Britannica entry sums up his life and his work. He was born at Karlstadt in Bavaria and died at Amsterdam. Little is known of his path beyond the towns he lived in, among them Vienna, Salzburg, Frankfurt, and Cologne, before he settled in Holland. There he earned his living chiefly by selling secret chemical and medical preparations.

For all his talk of universal solvents and other alchemist dreams, the entry credits him with real advances. He set out how to make hydrochloric acid from oil of vitriol and common salt, and praised the salt formed in the process, still called Glauber's salt. He made many other salts of lead, tin, iron, and other metals, and he pushed the use of his knowledge in medicine, dyeing, and farming.
britannica-1911-hagenbach-karl-rudolf:
Karl Rudolf Hagenbach, German church historian born on 4 March 1801 at Basel, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. His father worked as a doctor in that city. A Pestalozzian school gave the boy his first lessons. The gymnasium came next, and then the newly reshaped local university.

Early on he gave himself to the study of church teaching and to church service. At the same time he kept wide human tastes alive in many forms. Warm love for the old classics marked that breadth in him. The entry opens his life story on that double track of faith and letters. His later work as a historian of the church grew from those twin roots at Basel.
britannica-1911-hand-ferdinand-gotthelf:
Ferdinand Gotthelf Hand (1786–1851) was a German classical scholar. He was born at Plauen in Saxony on 15 February 1786. He studied at Leipzig. In 1810 he became professor at the Weimar gymnasium. In 1817 Jena made him professor of philosophy and Greek literature. He stayed at Jena until his death in 1851. His chief work edits Tursellinus on the Latin particles.

That edition, on Horatius Tursellinus' treatise, is unfinished. It appeared from 1829 to 1845. His textbook of Latin style shares its character. Both works are too abstruse for ordinary students. Hand was also an enthusiastic musician. His Ästhetik der Tonkunst appeared from 1837 to 1841. It first introduced musical aesthetics as a subject. W. E. Lawson translated its first part into English in 1880.
britannica-1911-haym-rudolf:
Rudolf Haym (1821–1901) was a German publicist and philosopher. He was born at Grünberg in Silesia on 5 October 1821. Halle and Berlin were his universities, for philosophy and theology. In 1848 he sat in the Frankfort National Assembly. He wrote an account of its proceedings from the Right Centre. From 1851 he lectured at Halle in literature and philosophy. A professorship followed in 1860.

His writings are biographical and critical. Modern German philosophy and literature are their main field. His history of the Romantic school appeared in 1870. Readers judged it masterly. Biographies of Humboldt, Hegel and Schopenhauer came from him. A Herder biography ran from 1877 to 1885. His memoirs, Erinnerungen, appeared in 1901. He died at St Anton on 27 August 1901. The entry is a compact notice of a scholar's output.
britannica-1911-mullner-amandus-gottfrie:
Amandus Gottfried Adolf Müllner (1774-1829) was a German dramatic poet from Langendorf. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica notes he was nephew of poet Gottfried August Bürger. Law study at Leipzig led to practice as an advocate at Weissenfels. A novel in 1799 and small comedies for a local stage came first.

Tragedies made his name across the German stage for years. Die Schuld in 1813 set the model for fate tragedies that followed. Such plays, ruled by doom, held the stage on his pattern. Later plays won less weight with crowds and critics alike. He also edited journals and wrote sharp, stinging reviews of others.
britannica-1911-pelf: Pelf is a word now used chiefly for money, and always in a scornful sense. Its brief word entry in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica traces the term to a sense of plunder or pillage. The Old French form pelfre likely comes from a Latin verb for stripping hair. That root sense of taking by force survives in the kindred word pilfer. Pilfer means to make small thefts, a lighter echo of the old plunder sense.
britannica-1911-subliminal-self:
Subliminal self is a phrase tied to psychical research and to one writer above all. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica credits its wide use to F W H Myers. His book Human Personality set out the idea at full length. In strict use the phrase means his full theory of the hidden self.

In loose use people apply it to any hidden mental work. The entry warns that mixing the two senses clouds clear thought. It sticks to the strict sense throughout its account. Background covers Fechner and his threshold idea, and the broad doubt among scholars about unseen mental states at that time.
britannica-1911-trendelenburg-friedrich-:
Friedrich Adolf Trendelenburg, a German philosopher who lived from 1802 to 1872, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was born at Eutin, near Lübeck, in November 1802. He read at Kiel, Leipzig, and Berlin. Plato and Aristotle drew him ever more strongly as a student.

His doctoral work of 1826 read Plato's doctrine through Aristotle's criticisms. He refused a classical chair at Kiel to tutor a minister's son instead. In his spare time he prepared a critical edition of Aristotle's work on the soul. In 1833 Berlin made him a professor, and a full professor four years later. For nearly forty years he taught with marked success there. He examined every candidate for the teaching profession in Prussia in his subjects. Late in life he clashed fiercely with Kuno Fischer over Kant's doctrine of space. Their pamphlet war filled the years before his death in 1872.
britannica-1911-virchow-rudolf:
Rudolf Virchow is the subject of a life entry in the 1911 Britannica. He was a German doctor and statesman who lived from 1821 to 1902. He was born in Pomerania, the son of a farmer and shopkeeper. He went to Berlin to study medicine at age seventeen. He took his degree in 1843. He then took a post at a large hospital in Berlin. Soon he was teaching at the school there.

His views on reform forced him to leave Berlin for a time. He taught at Wurzburg and built up its medical school. In 1856 Berlin called him back to lead its study of disease. The entry calls him the father of the modern study of disease. His core view held that each body is a sum of small living units. He died in Berlin in 1902 after a fall from a tram.
britannica-1911-weckherlin-georg-rudolf:
Georg Rudolf Weckherlin (1584-1653) was a German poet born at Stuttgart on 15 September 1584. He read law and settled at Stuttgart as secretary to Duke Johann Friedrich of Wurttemberg. In that post he went on missions to France and England. From 1620 to 1624 he lived in England in the service of the Palatinate. The English state seems to have used him as well.

In 1644 Weckherlin was made Secretary for Foreign Tongues in England. When the Commonwealth was set up, Milton took that post after him. He died in London on 13 February 1653. He was the most marked of the south German poets who paved the way for the new birth of German verse tied to the name of Martin Opitz. Two books of his odes and songs came out in 1618 and 1619. His models were the poets of the French Pleiade.
britannica-1911-werwolf:
Werwolf is the old word for a man who is said to turn into a wolf for a time or for good. The entry links the word to old forms that mean man and wolf. Such tales are treated as one kind of the broad belief in change of shape. Wolf tales are by far the most common form in Europe.

Greek myth gives the tale of Lycaon, who ate human flesh and was changed. Old writers tell of men who swam a lake, lived nine years as wolves, and then swam back. The piece also notes like tales from the east of Europe and from Armenia. Each tale is set out in plain terms.
britannica-1911-westphal-rudolf: Rudolf Westphal, a German classical scholar who lived from 1826 to 1892, is covered in a brief life entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Obernkirchen, he studied at Marburg and Tubingen and held chairs at Breslau and Moscow. His fame rests on his work on Greek music and metre. His chief books cover Greek metre, old rhythm, and the music of the Greek world. He also rendered Catullus and a play of Aristophanes into German.
britannica-1911-wilbrandt-adolf:
Adolf Wilbrandt was a German tale and stage writer who was born at Rostock in eighteen thirty-seven. He was the son of a teacher at that towns school of high rank. He first read law, then gave it up for words and the past. A degree and press work at Munich came next.

He roamed abroad, then set his home in Vienna and wed a stage star. In eighteen eighty-one he took charge of the court stage there for six years. Prizes for his grave plays came twice in his life. His shelf holds sad plays, gay plays, and a long line of tales.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-aloys-lutolf:
Aloys Lutolf, historian, was born at Gettnau near Willisau in 1824 and died at Lucerne in 1879. He studied at Schwyz's Jesuit College and Lucerne's Lyceum, keen on history. Politics barred serious study, so Lütolf and fellow students volunteered. He served as Lucerne private secretary and joined the Sonderbund's Ticino expedition. From 1847 to 1849 he read theology and history at Freiburg and Munich, ordained at Solothurn.

After mission service, he taught at St. Gall's cantonal school from 1852 to 1856. When the school closed, he became Lucerne parish priest. He became church history professor in 1858, Lucerne's St. Leodegar canon, and Solothurn seminary viceregent in 1864. In 1859 he began publishing St. Gall investigations. Chief are Legends, Customs and Tales from the Five Places (1865) and Heralds of the Faith in Switzerland before St. Gall (1870), a contribution to ancient Swiss history. His Life and Confessions of Schiffmann (1861) memorializes his master and covers Bishop Sailer and his Swiss school.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-arculf:
Arculf, a Frankish bishop of the later seventh century, is known through Bede's account of a pilgrimage that became a book. Some, such as Alexis de Gourgues, call him bishop of Périgueux, but most believe he belonged to some monastery. Bede relates that Arculf, returning from the Holy Land about 670 or 690, was cast by tempest on the Scottish shore and warmly received by Adamnan, abbot of Iona.

To Adamnan he gave a detailed narrative of his Holy Land travels, with plans and designs of the sanctuaries precise enough that Adamnan could produce a descriptive work. With help from other sources, Adamnan produced that work in three books on Jerusalem, Bethlehem, the chief towns of Palestine, and Constantinople. Adamnan gave a copy to Aldfrith, king of Northumbria, in 698. The work aims to report faithfully what Arculf actually saw, joined to an antiquary's zeal.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ceolwulf:
Ceolwulf, also spelled Ceolwulph or Ceolulph, was king of Northumbria and monk of Lindisfarne, dying at Lindisfarne in 764; his birth date and place are unknown. The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle traces his ancestry back through Cutha, Cuthwin, Leoldwald, Egwald, Aldhelm, and Ocga to Ida and Eoppa. Most authorities say Osric adopted him as heir in 729, though Harpsfeld says he succeeded Osred.

Learned and pious, he lacked the vigor and authority a ruler needs. Bede witnesses to his learning and piety in the opening chapter of his Ecclesiastical History, dedicated to the most glorious King Ceolwulph and sent for his approval. His subjects seized him in his second regnal year and confined him in a monastery, but he escaped and regained the throne. He made his cousin Egbert Bishop of York, and his feast day is 15 January.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cynewulf:
A literary entry examines Cynewulf, the Anglo-Saxon poet whose authorship is certain yet whose identity is not. He signed four poems by spelling his name in runic letters that read as sense within the verse. Who he was remains uncertain. Good reason links him with Cynewulf, Bishop of Lindisfarne.

A rival claim favours Cynulf, an ecclesiastic who signed the decrees of Clovesho in 803. But the chief argument against the bishop has been shown baseless. It claimed a debt to Alcuin's work of about 802. From his own runic passages we learn he knew revelry in a hall, was converted, and gave himself to sacred song, dreading past sins in old age. His certain poems are Christ, Elene, Juliana, and the Fates of the Apostles.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ernulf:
Ernulf, an architect from Beauvais in France, lived from 1040 until 1124. At Bec, Lanfranc was his teacher, and after Ernulf entered the Benedictine Order he lived long as a brother at Saint-Lucien in Beauvais. Lanfranc suggested the move that took him to England sometime after 1070, where he joined Canterbury's Christ Church monks. There Archbishop Anselm appointed him prior, and two higher posts followed: abbot of Peterborough in 1107, then bishop of Rochester in 1114.

At Canterbury he took down the eastern part of Lanfranc's church and raised a far grander building. The famous crypt, Our Lady of the Undercroft, belonged to that work, which reached as far as Trinity Tower. Peterborough and Rochester saw the same pattern: old buildings torn down, and new dormitories, refectories, and a chapter house put up. His Textus Roffensis, a large collection of documents about the Church of Rochester, came with several canonical and theological treatises.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-golden-calf:
The Golden Calf is an object of worship among the Hebrews, named chiefly in Exodus 32 for Aaron's molten calf and in 1 Kings 12 for Jeroboam's policy after the schism. The Hebrew term likely means a young bullock just arrived at maturity, not a calf in the strict sense. A Catholic Encyclopedia article follows two idolatries, one in the desert and one in the divided kingdom.

Impatient at Moses' long delay on the mount, the people asked Aaron for gods to go before them. He fashioned a molten bull from the golden earrings of women and children. Moses returned, destroyed the idol, ground it to dust, and made the Israelites drink from the brook. After the schism Jeroboam set up two golden calves at Bethel and Dan, likely as symbols of Yahweh, to keep northern pilgrims from Jerusalem.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ingulf:
Abbot of Croyland in Lincolnshire, Ingulf died there on 17 December 1109 after ruling the abbey for twenty-four years. He first appears as secretary to William the Conqueror, visiting England in 1051. Then he made a pilgrimage to Jerusalem. He entered the Norman house of Fontenelle, where the abbot made him prior. When Croyland fell vacant after Lanfranc deposed Abbot Ulfeytel, William himself had Ingulf named abbot in 1087.

Able and kind, Ingulf won his predecessor's release from confinement at Glastonbury and saw him back at Peterborough, his first house. Gout racked the abbot's health, and fire partly wrecked his church with its sacristies, vestments, and books, yet he governed with success. His abbacy also saw a notable burial at Croyland, closing a life spent between Norman courts and English cloisters.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-bertulf:
St. Bertulf was abbot of Bobbio, date of birth unknown. He died in 639 or 640. This entry follows the son of a pagan nobleman in Austrasia, a near relative of St. Arnulf of Metz, whose pious example led Bertulf to become a Christian. In 620 he entered the monastery of Luxeuil. A few years later he met Abbot Attala, visiting Luxeuil, and, with Abbot Eustace's permission, joined Attala's community at Bobbio in Italy.

Upon Attala's death in 627, Bobbio's monks elected Bertulf their abbot. Like his holy predecessor, he insisted on observing the austere rule St. Columban, Bobbio's founder, had introduced. He preached fearlessly against Arianism, firmly rooted in Italy under the Lombard kings. When Tortona's bishop tried to bring Bobbio under his jurisdiction, Bertulf hastened to Rome, where Pope Honorius received him with honour.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-theodulf:
Bishop and poet Theodulf of Orléans, Charlemagne's learned Goth, is the courtier-scholar portrayed here. Born in Spain about 760, dying at Angers on 18 December 821, he joined Charlemagne's court before 794, ranking next to Alcuin as its most distinguished and learned person. About 798 Charlemagne granted him Orléans bishopric and several abbeys.

Diocesan reform of clergy and people fills his two Capitularies, one of forty-six chapters, and schools drew his encouragement. In 798 he travelled with Leidrad of Lyons as royal missus dominicus to southern France, complaining in Versus contra judices of Frankish law's severity and warning judges. Filioque dispute saw him defend the Spirit's procession from Son as well as Father.
confidences-talks-with-a-young-girl-conc:
Confidences: Talks With a Young Girl Concerning Herself, by Edith B. Lowry, is dedicated to Mary Louise and opens with a secret told to a child called Violet. Every little flower, she learns, is a living being, and every plant a household. A thirsty flower tells its need by drooping its head, and thanks its waterer by lifting it again.

Nine short chapters build on the lesson: The Flower Babies, The Bird Babies, Mother's Baby, The Baby's Nest, Building the Nest, The Sign Language, Rest and Sleep, and Injury of the Nest. Reproduction is taught wholly by analogy until the closing talks. There a woman in normal health, the book says, who loves children and desires one, need fear no serious trouble; painless childbirth is held out as possible.
doe-osti-3009665-review-of-presentation-: Los Alamos review form LA-UR-25-32128, by Nikhil Seshadri, issued December 17, 2025, is a structured peer review of a SULI presentation by Carter Wolf on machine learning denoising of ARPES data. The reviewer found the presentation informative and well researched, praised the clear introduction and conclusion, and noted the honest documentation of attempts that worked and attempts that did not. It is a one-form review record, not a research report.
doe-osti-3374079-analysis-of-temperature:
INL/RPT-25-86932, an Idaho National Laboratory report, dated August 2025, by Kevin Tsai, Austin D. Fleming, and Devin D. Imholte studies how heat affects self-powered neutron detectors sitting in a gamma field. These small, rugged in-core sensors could serve in reactors hotter than 600 degrees Celsius, but earlier tests showed odd displacement currents tied to temperature. Tests at the Ohio State University Research Reactor pointed to low-energy electrons from gamma interactions as the cause.

To pin the effect down, the team ran heated gamma irradiations up to 750 degrees Celsius at the Advanced Test Reactor Gamma Facility. Repeated step tests climbed in 100-degree steps to 700 degrees. For one rhodium detector, displacement currents ran negative below 500 degrees and turned positive above it, a pattern that repeated across runs. Knowing where the sign flips helps users correct readings from hot cores.
fanny-herself:
Edna Ferber wrote Fanny Herself as a novel about Fanny Brandeis, a Jewish girl growing up in a Wisconsin town where her widowed mother runs a dry-goods bazaar. Fanny is bright, funny, and unsentimental, and she refuses the ladylike future others plan for her. After her mother dies, she leaves home and builds a career as a buyer for a Chicago mail-order house.

Ferber fills the middle chapters with the workings of that mail-order business, its bundle chutes, stock clerks, and orders bound for Alaska and Georgia. Fanny succeeds through nerve and taste, then faces a harder choice between money, ambition, and the people she loves. Readers get a sharp portrait of a self-made businesswoman in early twentieth-century America.
little-eyolf:
Henrik Ibsen wrote this play in Christiania during 1894. Copenhagen published it on December 11 that year. William Archer translated it and supplied this introduction. Archer notes Ibsen's correspondence offers few clues to its origins.

One character, the Rat-Wife, has a definite suggested model. An old woman killed rats at Ibsen's childhood school. She carried a little dog in a bag, Ibsen told Prozor. Children were said to have drowned following her, like Hamelin's piper. Archer admits very little anecdotic history attaches to the play. Prozor's French word infatuation puzzles him in Allmers's case.
richard-dare-s-venture-or-striking-out-f:
Edward Stratemeyer tells boys how Richard Dare struck out for himself, in a preface to the revised edition dated at Newark on March 1, 1899. The book is complete in itself, he says, yet opens his Bound to Succeed series. Readers and critics across the country had taken it warmly, to his surprise and thanks.

Richard is a country youth who finds nothing to do in his sleepy village and goes to New York to seek his fortune. He has almost no cash, but backbone and his mother's Christian teaching in plenty. City life proves no bed of roses, and snares meet him once he gains a footing. The New York street scenes, Stratemeyer adds, are taken from life.
the-complete-poems-of-sir-thomas-moore-c:
Sir Thomas Moore's complete poems, collected by himself with explanatory notes, open with a biographical sketch by William M. Rossetti. The sketch begins with the poet's birth in Dublin on the 28th of May, 1780, as the date is printed there.

His father was a grocer and spirit-retailer, called a spirit-grocer in Ireland. Thomas was schooled by Mr. Samuel Whyte, once Sheridan's first teacher, a man of more than average literary culture. Whyte encouraged acting among the boys, and Moore, bright and lively by nature, became a favorite and a leader in the school plays. His gift for verse showed early. In 1790 he wrote an epilogue for a piece acted at Lady Borrows's house in Dublin, and at fourteen he published a sonnet to Whyte in a Dublin magazine. Rossetti frames the poems with that rise from a tradesman's son to a national poet.
the-golden-calf: M. E. Braddon wrote The Golden Calf. It is a novel. The title page names Braddon as author of Lady Audley's Secret and Aurora Floyd. It names Vixen and Ishmael as well. Only front matter is present here. It gives the title page and a contents list. The heads open with The Articled Pupil. One head is blunt: I Am Going to Marry for Money. Later heads name Wendover Abbey, a birthday feast, and a solemn league. They name Kingthorpe society and The True Knight.
the-great-panjandrum-himself: The Great Panjandrum Himself is one of R. Caldecott's Picture Books. Frederick Warne and Company published the series. Only the opening pages are present here: the front cover and the first picture pages. The book is a nonsense rhyme told in pictures. A lady goes into the garden to cut a cabbage-leaf, to make an apple-pie. The words come a line or two at a time, under the pictures. No more of the rhyme is present.
the-half-back-a-story-of-school-football: Ralph Henry Barbour wrote The Half-Back, a story of school, football, and golf, with pictures by B. West Clinedinst. The dedication speaks to every American boy who loves honest, manly sport. Chapter titles in the contents include The Boy in the Straw Hat, Station Road and River Path, Outfield West, The Head Coach, The Practice Game, and The Golf Tournament. Nothing past the front matter is present here.
the-history-of-thomas-ellwood-written-by:
The History of Thomas Ellwood was written by Ellwood himself. George Routledge and Sons printed the edition in 1885. Henry Morley wrote an introduction for it. Morley presents the life of the simple Quaker with praise. The book makes Ellwood known with frankness, he says. It also brings a bygone time close to the reader. It even helps the reader come near to Milton in daily life.

Ellwood was born in 1639, in the reign of Charles the First. His story runs to 1683, when he was forty-four. He outlived the days of trouble recorded in the book. He died on the first of March 1713, aged seventy-four. His house stood at Hunger Hill.
the-son-of-the-wolf:
Jack London's 1900 collection gathers nine tales of the far north. Among them are The White Silence, The Men of Forty Mile, In a Far Country, and The Wisdom of the Trail. An Odyssey of the North completes the set. The title story gives the volume its name, and the harsh Yukon world runs through the whole set.

The White Silence opens with Mason tending a failing sled dog, Carmen, while Malemute Kid thaws frozen bread by the fire. Ruth, Mason's Indian wife, listens in silence. Two hundred miles of trail lie ahead, with six days of food for the people and none for the dogs, so hunger shapes every choice the party faces.
toward-the-gulf: Edgar Lee Masters gathered poems under his title in a contents list running from the title poem through lake boats, cities of the plain, Johnny Appleseed, and a loom. Dialogue at Perko's, Sir Galahad, St. Deseret, and Victor Rafolski on art appear among the titles. Later poems treat dahlias, the Grand River marshes, Delilah, France, Christmas at Indian Point, and a clinical lecture by Dr. Scudder. A contents list alone is held in this record, so Masters's poems themselves are not shown.
when-a-man-comes-to-himself:
Woodrow Wilson wrote the essay When a Man Comes to Himself in 1901. Wilson, who later served as President of the United States, treats a quiet inner change. A man comes to himself, he says, not only after wild or foolish years. The change can follow private trials that no one else has seen.

Such a man stops centering all his plans on himself. He sees the world as it is and finds his true place in it. Old illusions drop away, both the rosy ones and the dark ones. He learns his own pace and the roads he must run. Wilson calls the loss of illusion a gain, since the new light guides rather than cheats.
